overview.text: A sword is a hand-held weapon built around a long blade joined to a hilt; its grip and guard help the user hold and control it. Swords are not one fixed design: blade shape and edge distinguish forms intended chiefly for cutting, thrusting, or both, including curved sabres and straight double-edged blades. Their designs changed with fighting needs; for example, one fifteenth-century European sword at the Met has a pointed, double-edged blade suited to thrusting and slashing against armor. Historically swords served as weapons, but some also carried social meaning: decorated and ceremonial forms show their place in status and dress as well as combat.

key_facts.text: A typical sword has a blade and a hilt; the hilt commonly includes a grip, guard, and pommel.
Blade shape and construction vary with intended use: examples include cutting blades, narrow thrusting blades, and curved blades designed for cutting.
The Met’s two-handed sword, dated about 1400–1450, has a long, pointed, double-edged blade designed for thrusting and slashing; the museum says it could be used against plate armor.
The Met’s circa-1450 European sword has a simple cross-shaped hilt and a rounded blade tip; the museum identifies it as primarily a slashing weapon that could also thrust.
Sword types include broadswords, hand-and-a-half swords, sabres, rapiers, ceremonial swords, and specialized forms from Asia and the Islamic world.
